description: FlameForgeTeam is a multidisciplinary team with expertise in AI, backend development, application engineering, and education research. We combine technology and research to turn complex data into meaningful insights. For Flame in Freefall, we aim to build an AI-powered platform for exploring microgravity combustion data and delivering clear fire-safety insights for future human space missions.
summary:
IGNIS is a web dashboard that helps researchers find, compare and question NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments. NASA has decades of fire research in its PSI database, but it is hard to search and hard to compare. IGNIS puts the investigations in one place, with sources linked next to every fact.

What makes it different is the habitat ranking. Future Moon bases and pressurized rovers will use more oxygen than Earth air, at lower pressure. So we ask a practical question: which investigations tested conditions closest to a given habitat? For example, in the ISS cabin ranking, FLEX comes first with a score of 0.203, calculated from 55 of its 274 tests. The page shows the formula, and a record with no relevant tests is marked “no tests” instead of getting a zero.

IGNIS does not predict fire risk. It helps people find the right evidence faster and see where it is thin.
details:
IGNIS has six parts:

  • Overview: shows how many investigations, files and publications are indexed.
  • Explore: keyword and filter search, with a reason shown for each match.
  • Compare: puts 2 to 4 investigations side by side, with missing values shown as “not reported”.
  • Research Map: a coverage matrix showing which topics and fuels are well covered and which are sparse in our dataset.
  • Habitat ranking: ranks investigations for four habitats: a spacesuit (4.3 psia, pure oxygen), the ISS cabin, NASA’s exploration atmosphere (8.2 psia, 34% oxygen) and a reduced-pressure staged cabin (10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen).
  • AI Copilot: answers questions with citations back to the source records and says when the evidence is missing.

How the habitat ranking works

The backend scores each investigation by how many of its tests match a habitat’s conditions:

score = (tests_full + 0.5 × tests_partial) / tests_total

A test counts as full when both oxygen and pressure are in range. It counts as partial when oxygen is in range but pressure was not reported. The page displays this formula exactly as the backend sends it, so users can see how every number was produced. The CSV export of the underlying tests lets them check the numbers themselves.

Why this matters

Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration and pressure, and future crew habitats will not match the conditions of most past experiments. Researchers and engineers need to see quickly which studies are relevant to those atmospheres. The ranking is meant to start that search, not to replace engineering review.

Scientific honesty

We tried to build trust into the interface:

  • Missing data is shown as “Not reported”, never as zero.
  • Charts are drawn only when values share the same name and unit.
  • A “gap” means “nothing in the indexed dataset”, not “no research exists”.
  • The AI answers only from retrieved records and never declares a material safe or predicts fire behavior.
  • PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet, so we do not present any result as lunar or Martian gravity.

Tools used

  • Front-end: Next.js 14 (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Axios and lucide-react.
  • Backend: databasewith postgresql hosted on supabase, Pyhton based fast api skeleton hosted on render. It serves investigations, tests, habitats, ranking, comparison, coverage analytics and the CSV export
  • AI: [name the model/provider you used, for example Gemini], called only from the backend, so no keys reach the browser.
  • Data: public NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) records and the challenge resources.

Creative approach

The home page shows a teardrop flame on Earth next to a spherical flame in free fall, which is the central idea of the challenge. The interface is designed like a mission-control dashboard, with the source of every claim shown beside it.
